question:
What does matrix[True, False] do in numpy?

For example, I have matrix=np.array([[1,2],[3,4]]) . When I use boolean filtration in Numpy like: matrix[[True,False]] , I understand how's it works - I'll get the first row. But when I use something like: matrix[True, False] , I get empty parentheses. I guess, in this case boolean values means which dimension I want to use, because if I write: matrix[True, True] , then I'll get the whole matrix, but if I use: matrix[True, True, False] , then again I'll get empty parentheses, even though I have a 2D array. How does this actually work?
reference_answer: This is a very weird case. It is in fact tested , but I don't think the behavior is documented anywhere. If you index an array with any number of True scalars, the result is equivalent to arr[np.newaxis] : it contains all the original array's data, but with an extra length-1 axis at the start of its shape. If you index an array with any number of boolean scalars, at least one of which is False , you get an empty result. The result has the shape of the original array, except with an extra length-0 axis at the start of the shape. The normal case for a boolean index is for the index array and the original array to have the same shape. The desired behavior in the normal case is to produce a 1D array containing all elements of the original array corresponding to True cells in the index array. For >=1D boolean index arrays, this is equivalent to substituting index.nonzero() in place of the index array. But nonzero() is a little weird for 0D arrays. Instead, 0D boolean arraylikes (including ordinary boolean scalars) have special handling. A comment in the code describes the special handling as follows: /* * This can actually be well defined. A new axis is added, * but at the same time no axis is "used". So if we have True, * we add a new axis (a bit like with np.newaxis). If it is * False, we add a new axis, but this axis has 0 entries. */ And when you index an array with a single boolean scalar index and nothing else, the comment accurately describes the behavior. In particular, it does the right thing in the case that motivates the special handling: array(5.0)[True] produce arra
llm_attempt: A boolean array/list, e.g. matrix[[True, False]], is advanced indexing: it's treated as a mask over axis 0, so you get row 0. A bare Python bool used as its own element inside an index tuple works differently: each scalar bool is a 0-d boolean index that does NOT consume an existing axis. Instead it inserts a new axis, sized 1 if True (like a conditional np.newaxis, keeping that slice) or sized 0 if False (making that axis empty). So matrix[True, False] inserts a size-1 axis then a size-0 axis, giving shape (1,0,2,2) - empty. matrix[True, True] inserts two size-1 axes, shape (1,1,2,2), which still holds the whole matrix (not empty). matrix[True, True, False] inserts three such axes (sizes 1,1,0) the same way, regardless of matrix only having 2 real dimensions, because scalar bools never index into existing dimensions - they only prepend new axes based on truthiness, and don't count toward "too many indices" errors. Rule of thumb: use an array/list of bools to mask an axis; scalar bools in a tuple do newaxis-style insertion instead.

question:
Why does asyncio.gather() not cancel pending tasks when one task fails?

I'm using asyncio.gather to run multiple coroutines in parallel. When one coroutine raises an exception, I expect the remaining tasks to be cancelled. However, they continue running. import asyncio async def worker(id): await asyncio.sleep(1) if id == 2: raise ValueError("Failing task") return id async def main(): tasks = [worker(i) for i in range(5)] try: await asyncio.gather(*tasks) except Exception as e: print("Error:", e) asyncio.run(main())
reference_answer: That has never been the proposal of asyncio.gather - rather, it is a simple mechanism to fire several co-routines concurrently and fetch all the results at once, and an exception is understood as a "result" in this context. asyncio.wait will offer one more control, though, it is also aimed at "let things run" - as in not all workflows a single failure would mean all sibling coroutines should be cancelled. But as it has the explicit return_when argument, which can be set to FIRST_COMPLETED it can work in scenarios when that cancelling is interesting; And finally, there is asyncio.TaskGroup which default (and only) behavior is exactly that of cancelling all sibling tasks when the first one errors: as taskgroups are somewhat poised as "the asyncio.gather successor for the obvious way to do asyncio concurrency" - it follows your desired pattern. Although it didn't "catch" that much - I suspect that is because the cancel all siblings behavior is only desired for a minority of real-world use cases. Therefore, you probably should want to use asyncio.TaskGroup instead of asyncio.gather . (If I would try to answer the "why" like you asked, it is rather subjective, but it could be because that was a pattern that did not occur as being the default for the authors at the time, but it did so to the authors of the much more recent, trio-inspired asyncio.TaskGroup . Your example would be like this: import asyncio import traceback async def worker(id): await asyncio.sleep(0.5) if id == 2: raise ValueError("Failing task") # also, make yielding to the loop _after_ the exception # had occurre

question:
ray.tune: Tracked actor is not managed

from ray import tune from ray.tune.search.optuna import OptunaSearch from ray.tune.integration.pytorch_lightning import TuneReportCheckpointCallback from pytorch_lightning import Trainer from pytorch_lightning.callbacks import EarlyStopping from data_module import DataModule from fcnn_regressor import FCNNRegressor from typing import Any dm = DataModule(X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test, batch_size=2028) def train_model(config: dict[str, Any]) -> None: model = FCNNRegressor( input_dim=X_train.shape[1], hidden_dim1=config["hidden_dim1"], hidden_dim2=config["hidden_dim2"], dropout_prob=config["dropout_prob"], lr=config["lr"], weight_decay=config["weight_decay"], ) trainer = Trainer( max_epochs=100, callbacks=[ EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", patience=5, mode="min"), TuneReportCheckpointCallback({"val_loss": "val_loss"}, on="validation_end") ], ) trainer.fit(model, datamodule=dm) search_space = { "hidden_dim1": tune.randint(64, 257), "hidden_dim2": tune.sample_from( lambda cfg: np.random.randint(16, cfg["hidden_dim1"] // 2 + 1)), "dropout_prob": tune.uniform(0.1, 0.4), "lr": tune.loguniform(1e-5, 1e-2), "weight_decay": tune.loguniform(1e-6, 1e-2), } optuna = OptunaSearch(metric="val_loss", mode="min") tuner = tune.Tuner( train_model, param_space=search_space, tune_config=tune.TuneConfig(num_samples=20, search_alg=optuna), ) results = tuner.fit() print(results.get_best_result("val_loss", "min").metrics) Why there is the following error: --------------------------------------------------------------------------- ValueError Traceback (most recent call last) File ~/pyenvs/base/li
llm_attempt: "Tracked actor is not managed" is an internal Ray Tune actor-bookkeeping error, and it's usually a symptom, not the root cause - it means a trial's actor died or errored before Tune could register/track it properly. Check the full trial error log (~/ray_results/.../error.txt) for the real underlying exception. Likely causes here: (1) ray.tune.integration.pytorch_lightning.TuneReportCheckpointCallback is the old, largely unmaintained integration path for recent Ray/Lightning versions - switch to ray.train.lightning.RayTrainReportCallback with ray.train.lightning.prepare_trainer; (2) a version mismatch between ray, pytorch-lightning, and optuna; (3) an exception thrown inside train_model or the search space itself (e.g. tune.sample_from's lambda uses np - confirm numpy is actually imported in that module) that crashes the trial immediately. Try running train_model directly (no Tuner) with one fixed config first to confirm it works standalone, then reintroduce Tune/Optuna with pinned, mutually-compatible package versions.

question:
Free Python TTS libraries that won't fail after deployment

Is there a free python tts library with mp3 download function and won't fail after deployment?? I have tried various libraries like gtts, edge-tts, pttsx3 and piper-tts and they work locally but fails after deployment on render. I actually need a tts library for a web app that can handle large text of about 3000 words per generation and can convert those words into an mp3 audio file for download.
reference_answer: how it failed? Did you get error message? Maybe you should catch error and read it. Maybe it needs only to install some C/C+ library. If modules gtts, edge-tts, pttsx3 and piper-tts had problem then I expect other modules will also have problem.
llm_attempt: No library is guaranteed to work on every host; the failures you're seeing on Render usually come from either missing system binaries (pyttsx3 needs espeak/espeak-ng installed at the OS level, which Render's default Python environment doesn't include) or blocked/rate-limited outbound calls (gTTS and edge-tts both hit external web endpoints, which can fail or throttle on shared hosting). For something genuinely self-contained, Piper TTS is a real offline neural engine - but you must bundle the .onnx voice model files inside your deployment image (not fetch them at runtime) and install the piper binary as a build step, so nothing needs network access when generating speech. Write raw audio to WAV, then convert to mp3 with pydub + ffmpeg (add ffmpeg as a system package too). If your Render plan supports a Dockerfile-based service rather than the native buildpack, use that - it gives you control to apt-get install espeak-ng/ffmpeg and vendor piper's model files, which is the actual fix, not a different pip package.

question:
Get unique elements in multiple List columns

Consider a DataFrame with multiple list columns, for instance: df = pl.DataFrame({ "a": [range(1,3), range(5,10)], "b": [range(4,9), range(6,11)] }) Let's print it: with pl.Config(set_fmt_table_cell_list_len=100): print(df) shape: (2, 2) ┌─────────────────┬──────────────────┐ │ a ┆ b │ │ --- ┆ --- │ │ list[i64] ┆ list[i64] │ ╞═════════════════╪══════════════════╡ │ [1, 2] ┆ [4, 5, 6, 7, 8] │ │ [5, 6, 7, 8, 9] ┆ [6, 7, 8, 9, 10] │ └─────────────────┴──────────────────┘ I want to extract the unique values contained in the table. I came up with: # Concatenate the columns c = df.get_column("a").to_list() + df.get_column("b").to_list() # Flatten the columns and extract unique values flat_list = {x for xs in c for x in xs} Is there a faster way? Because I think the to_list() function is slow.
reference_answer: Assuming you want a Python set back, like in your example... unique is done in Polars (even though the call to set() will remove duplicates) in case the number of elements in large (better performance in Polars) df = pl.DataFrame({ "a": [range(1,3), range(5,10)], "b": [range(4,9), range(6,11)] }) set(df.select(pl.concat_list("a", "b").explode().unique()).to_series()) # {1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10}
llm_attempt:
Stay in Polars/Arrow instead of pulling to Python lists first. Concatenate the two Series and explode+unique natively:

unique_vals = (
    pl.concat([df.get_column("a"), df.get_column("b")])
    .explode()
    .unique()
)

or across both columns via concat_list:

df.select(pl.concat_list(["a", "b"]).alias("x")).select(pl.col("x").explode().unique())

Both run entirely in Rust over the Series, avoiding the Python-level to_list() + set comprehension, which forces full materialization into Python objects plus a Python-level loop - that's the actual slow part, not Polars. .explode() flattens the list columns and .unique() dedups; only call .to_list() at the very end if you need a plain Python list.

question:
Can't see color in Visual Studio Code

I'm following "Hands on Large Language Models" by Alammar. One of the examples is: from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer colors_list = [ '102;194;165', '252;141;98', '141;160;203', '231;138;195', '166;216;84', '255;217;47' ] def show_tokens(sentence, tokenizer_name): tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(tokenizer_name) token_ids = tokenizer(sentence).input_ids for idx, t in enumerate(token_ids): print( f'\x1b[0;30;48;2;{colors_list[idx % len(colors_list)]}m' + tokenizer.decode(t) + '\x1b[0m', end=' ' ) text = """ English and CAPITALIZATION 🎵 鸟 show_tokens False None elif == >= else: two tabs:" " Three tabs: " " 12.0*50=600 """ show_tokens(text, "bert-base-uncased") Which is supposed to show up as: However, in Visual Studio Code I see it as:
reference_answer: You’re running this inside a Jupyter Notebook, and that’s the key detail here. The color formatting in your code uses ANSI escape codes, which are designed to work in standard terminals like your system shell (e.g., Terminal on macOS/Linux, or Command Prompt/Powershell on Windows). These terminals understand those escape sequences and display colored backgrounds properly. However, Jupyter Notebooks don’t natively support ANSI color codes in the same way, they just show the raw escape sequences or ignore them altogether. That’s why it looks off or doesn’t render as expected. How to fix or work around this: Try running the script in a regular terminal (outside of Jupyter/VS Code) If you’re set on seeing it within a Jupyter-like environment, you can explore using libraries like rich or IPython.display tools that are more Jupyter-compatible for output formatting Or, if you’re just debugging tokenization, consider printing token info with regular text output or using HTML output via IPython.display.HTML
llm_attempt: This is almost always about where the output is rendered, not the ANSI codes. VS Code's integrated terminal supports 24-bit truecolor ANSI escapes fine, but the Debug Console, the Jupyter/interactive output panel, and some "Output" tabs don't render ANSI color - they show raw escape sequences or strip them, which looks like missing/garbled color. Make sure you run the script via the terminal-based runner (the Run Python File button, or Ctrl+F5 "Run Without Debugging", which opens a real integrated terminal), not by hitting the debug (bug icon) button, which sends output to the Debug Console instead. Also confirm you're not running it inside a Jupyter cell/interactive window, which has the same limitation. If it's still wrong in the actual integrated terminal, check the terminal profile isn't a legacy cmd.exe session with virtual terminal processing disabled - use the default PowerShell or Windows Terminal profile.

question:
how to check if pid has rolled over?

I am writing a program that will periodically scan all processes on a machine. I want to cache as much as possible to avoid any system load. I can list all available pids on a machine with ls /proc/[0-9]* and then iterate over the list. What do I use as the key of the cache to protect against pid number re-use? In other words, consider the following python code, that opens two pid directories in some different points in time. What is needed to compare the directories to check if they refer to the same process? pid_dir_fd1 = os.open("/proc/123", os.O_RDONLY) time.sleep(1) pid_dir_fd2 = os.open("/proc/123", os.O_RDONLY) print(are_pid_dirs_equal(pid_dir_fd1, pid_dir_fd2)) I can't use pidfd as I want to access /proc/<pid>/{cmdline,exe,stat,status} files to collect information about processes. Or I can? I do not know how is it possible to connect pidfd with the /proc/<pid>/files . My current idea is to compare the starttime field of stat file of processe: def read_text(file: str, dir_fd: int): with os.open(file, dir_fd=dir_fd) as f: return f.read() def stat_field(statstr: str, idx: int): return int(statstr.split(")")[-1].split()[idx - 3]) pid_dir_fd1 = os.open("/proc/123", os.O_RDONLY) starttime1 = stat_field(read_text("stat", pid_dir_fd1), 22) time.sleep(1) pid_dir_fd2 = os.open("/proc/123", os.O_RDONLY) starttime2 = stat_field(read_text("stat", pid_dir_fd2), 22) if create_time1 == create_time2: print("both directories are equal") else: print("pid_dir_fd1 died in the meantime") Is there something better?
reference_answer: My thoughts: When you scan /proc , PIDs can indeed be reused after a process exits. So for /proc/123 at one time may refer to a different process later. In order to cache or track processes safely, you would need a unique per-process identifier that doesn't change during its lifetime. Hope this makes sense... The reliable way is to combine the PID with the process start time from /proc/[pid]/stat (field 22) would be the below: (pid, start_time) which uniquely identifies a process for the duration of the system boot. I have a sudo code below if needed: import os def read_stat_starttime(pid): with open(f"/proc/{pid}/stat") as f: stat_fields = f.read().split(")") # field 22 (1-based) return int(stat_fields[-1].split()[20]) pid = 123 start1 = read_stat_starttime(pid) # ... later ... start2 = read_stat_starttime(pid) # True => same process, False => PID reused print(start1 == start2) Additionally, if you wish to have uniqueness across reboots, then you could consider including the system boot ID with something like the below. boot_id = open("/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id").read().strip() unique_id = (boot_id, pid, start1)
llm_attempt:
Simplest robust check: don't parse stat at all - compare the inode of the open /proc/<pid> directory file descriptors. Each time the kernel reuses a pid number for a new process, /proc/<pid> is backed by a fresh, distinct inode; the old one disappears when the original process exits. So:

st1 = os.fstat(pid_dir_fd1)
st2 = os.fstat(pid_dir_fd2)
same_process = st1.st_ino == st2.st_ino and st1.st_dev == st2.st_dev

That's cheaper than reading and parsing stat's starttime field and relies on the same underlying guarantee. Your starttime approach is also correct in principle - (pid, starttime) is the canonical unique process identity per proc(5) - just double check your field parsing is robust (comm can contain spaces/parens, but indexing from the ')' as you did is the standard-safe way). pidfd (os.pidfd_open, Linux 5.3+) is the newer race-free primitive, but it's mainly for detecting exit via poll/select, not for tagging cached per-process data - inode or starttime comparison is simpler for your use case.

question:
Python treemap with first level as color and legend rather than labels

I would like to try and create treemaps in Python that look similar to these ones : First example of what I'm aiming for Second example of what I'm aiming for (These examples come from this webpage ) Or similar to what you can make in R using the treemap package : https://r-graph-gallery.com/235-treemap-with-subgroups.html What I like about those is that the colors allow to easily see the first level and its size, but only the 2nd level squares are represented. I feel it makes for easier reading than what i am currently able to make (see below) #test data import pandas as pd product = ["Pins", "Binders", "Paper", "Pins", "Binders", "Paper"] city = ["Amsterdam", "Amsterdam", "Amsterdam", "Brussels", "Brussels", "Brussels"] sales = [6, 4, 1, 5, 3, 1] df = pd.DataFrame( dict(product=product, city=city, sales=sales) ) df product city sales 0 Pins Amsterdam 6 1 Binders Amsterdam 4 2 Paper Amsterdam 1 3 Pins Brussels 5 4 Binders Brussels 3 5 Paper Brussels 1 I tried using plotly : import plotly.express as px fig = px.treemap(df, path=['city', 'product'], values='sales') fig.update_layout(margin = dict(t=50, l=25, r=25, b=25)) fig.show() Treemap using plotly I don't like the style of this treemap, with the first level shown and the 2nd level smaller inside it. I would like the second level to completely fill the area of the first level. I also tried using squarify, with the color set as the first level (squarify only allows for 1 level if I understand correctly) : import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns import squarify fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 8)) ax.set_a
reference_answer: If you are just wanting to remove the spacing between squares completely, setting the parameter of squarify.plot(... pad=False) will suffice. But I noticed your examples still had spacing even though you said what you had 'are not grouped together', so you don't want it completely removed? I am also noticing that your examples put everything into column groups. Do you not want overlapping columns like this?: If you want really narrow 'borders', then add a line border and make the line border match the background color: pad=False, linewidth=1, edgecolor="white", You can use this for the legend: import matplotlib.patches as mpatches legend_patches = [mpatches.Patch(color=colors[i], label=city[i]) for i in range(len(city))] plt.legend(handles=legend_patches, loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.10, 1)) Adjust parameters of bbox_to_anchor if you want to shift the legend outside the boundaries of the squarify display. The legend might get clipped depending on where you put it, so add plt.tight_layout() before plt.show() if you want to auto adjust the view window to not cut off the legend.
llm_attempt:
squarify only lays out one flat level, so build the leaf-level layout yourself and color by the parent group instead of nesting boxes. Sort by group then value, run squarify on the leaf sizes only, and color each rectangle by its parent (city), with a manual legend instead of group labels:

import squarify, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Patch
d = df.sort_values(["city","sales"], ascending=[True,False])
norm = squarify.normalize_sizes(d["sales"], 100, 100)
rects = squarify.squarify(norm, 0, 0, 100, 100)
colors = {c: plt.cm.tab10(i) for i,c in enumerate(d["city"].unique())}
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for r,(_,row) in zip(rects, d.iterrows()):
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((r["x"],r["y"]), r["dx"], r["dy"], color=colors[row["city"]], ec="white"))
    ax.text(r["x"]+r["dx"]/2, r["y"]+r["dy"]/2, row["product"], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0,100); ax.set_ylim(0,100); ax.axis("off")
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(color=v,label=k) for k,v in colors.items()], bbox_to_anchor=(1,1))

This yields only leaf rectangles, colored/legended by top-level group - Plotly's px.treemap can't do this since it always draws parent boxes too.

question:
Parallel processing with arguments to modify

I need to parallelize a function that modifies values of one of the arguments. For example modify this simple code: def Test(i, a, length): if i % 2 == 0: for x in range(0, length, 2): a[x] = 2 else: for x in range(1, length, 2): a[x] = 1 a0 = numpy.ndarray(shape=10, dtype=numpy.uint8) Test(0, a, a.shape[0]) Test(1, a, a.shape[0]) print(a) I tried to use joblib using Parallel(n_jobs=2)(delayed(Test)(i, a, 10) for i in range(2)) and multiprocessing.Pool with: with multiprocessing.Pool(processes=2) as Pool: data = [(0, a, a.shape[0]), (1, a, a.shape[0])] Pool.starmap(Test, data) But both solutions do not work because they fork the data, so the parameters do not get modified. What would be my options to do such parallelization?
reference_answer: We use two functions: np_array_to_shared_array : Takes a numpy array and initializes a multiprocessing.Array instance with the contents of the numpy array. shared_array_to_np_array : Takes a multiprocessing.Array instance created with np_array_to_shared_array and reconstructs a numpy array whose buffer is the sharable multiprocessing.Array instance. We then create our multiprocessing pool specifying a pool initializer that is passed a multiprocessi.Array instance created with np_array_to_shared_array and then using shared_array_to_np_array reconstructs the sharable numpy array for each process in the pool as a global variable 'a': import numpy as np import multiprocessing def np_array_to_shared_array(np_array: np.ndarray, lock: bool=True ) -> multiprocessing.Array: """Initialize a multiprocessing.Array instance with the contents of a numpy array.""" shared_array = multiprocessing.Array('B', np_array.nbytes, lock=lock) buffer = shared_array.get_obj() if lock else shared_array arr = np.frombuffer(buffer, np_array.dtype) arr[:] = np_array.flatten(order='C') return shared_array def shared_array_to_np_array(shared_array: multiprocessing.Array, shape: tuple[int], dtype: object ) -> np.ndarray: """Initialize a numpy array using a multiprocessing.Array instance as the buffer.""" buffer = ( shared_array.get_obj() if getattr(shared_array, 'get_obj', None) else shared_array ) return np.ndarray(shape, dtype=dtype, buffer=buffer) def init_pool(shared_array, shape, dtype): global a a = shared_array_to_np_array(shared_array, shape, dtype) def test(i): len = a.shape[0] if i % 2 == 0: for x
llm_attempt:
multiprocessing forks (or spawns + pickles) each worker, so every process gets its own private copy of a - writes never propagate back to the parent, which is exactly what you're seeing with both joblib and Pool.starmap. To actually share and mutate memory across processes you need real shared memory, not a copied argument:

from multiprocessing import Process, shared_memory
import numpy as np
shm = shared_memory.SharedMemory(create=True, size=10)
a = np.ndarray((10,), dtype=np.uint8, buffer=shm.buf)

def Test(i, shm_name, length):
    ex = shared_memory.SharedMemory(name=shm_name)
    arr = np.ndarray((length,), dtype=np.uint8, buffer=ex.buf)
    arr[i % 2::2] = 2 if i % 2 == 0 else 1
    ex.close()

procs = [Process(target=Test, args=(i, shm.name, 10)) for i in range(2)]
[p.start() for p in procs]; [p.join() for p in procs]

multiprocessing.Array/RawArray works similarly for simpler ctypes cases. Alternatively, since numpy releases the GIL during array operations, just use threads (concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor) - they share memory natively, no serialization needed, and the GIL won't bottleneck this kind of workload.

question:
Is there a way to download DEM data of Geo-Referenced .tif satellite imagery tiles?

I have a satellite imagery dataset called SEN12MS-CR. It contains Sentinel 1 (SAR) and Sentinel 2 cloudy and cloud free imagery in .tif format. Its split into 169 ROIs over the globe, with each ROI being split into patches. The dataset contains 122,218 patch triplets with 256x256 px size. I need to download a DEM for essentially every patch in this dataset. I there a way to do it that I'm missing? I've written a script that iterates over the whole dataset and uses py3dep library to download the DEMs, but its saying its going to take about 60 hours. I know its a large dataset, but given the fact that each DEM 'patch' would be approx. 5kb, it shouldn't take this long. Is there a better method that I'm missing?
llm_attempt: Requesting a DEM per 256x256 patch is almost certainly what's slow - each py3dep call is a separate network round trip, and with 122k patches that per-request overhead dominates, not the actual data volume. Since your patches are grouped into only 169 ROIs, request the DEM once per ROI (covering the full bounding box of all patches in that ROI, padded a bit) instead of once per patch - about 169 requests instead of 122k. Then crop each patch's DEM locally and fast with rasterio (rasterio.windows.from_bounds or rasterio.mask) against the single downloaded ROI raster, no further network calls needed, and reuse it across every patch that shares that ROI. If ROI-level 3DEP queries are still slow, consider a bulk source built for large-area downloads instead of many small point queries - e.g. AWS's public Terrain Tiles / Copernicus GLO-30 on registry.opendata.aws, or OpenTopography's bulk API.

question:
Alembic Multitenant Aws

I'm building a multi-tenant SaaS with multiple databases, one per tenant in the AWS environment. I'm facing the issue of how to manage migration versioning so that all tenants have the same schema. The idea would be to generate the migration on my local machine by comparing it with the last generated version, and then deploy it so that all tenant databases are updated correctly. However, I'm not able to maintain a general schema to compare against. Is it possible to do this without creating a public control instance? The section of my code responsible for running the migrations is shown below. The initial migration worked perfectly, but now I'm running into an error when trying to generate new migrations because I receive the message: ERROR [alembic.util.messaging] Target database is not up to date. FAILED: Target database is not up to date. def run_migrations_online(): import sys is_generating = any(cmd in sys.argv for cmd in ["revision"]) if is_generating: from sqlalchemy import create_engine connectable = create_engine("sqlite:///:memory:") with connectable.connect() as connection: context.configure( connection=connection, target_metadata=target_metadata, compare_type=True, compare_server_default=True, render_as_batch=False, ) with context.begin_transaction(): context.run_migrations() return tenants = tenant_config_manager.list_all_tenants() if not tenants: return success_count = 0 error_count = 0 for tenant_id in tenants: try: db_url = tenant_config_manager.get_database_url(tenant_id) if not db_url: error_count += 1 continue from sqlalchemy import create_engine connecta
reference_answer: You can use session-manager provided by AWS Systems manager to perform port-forwarding to the RDS using bastion host EC2. Ref: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/securely-connect-to-an-amazon-rds-or-amazon-ec2-database-instance-remotely-with-your-preferred-gui/
llm_attempt: Standard pattern: don't autogenerate against each live tenant DB. Keep one reference/"template" database - it needn't be public-facing, an ephemeral sqlite or a private dev Postgres you control is fine - that always reflects the current head of your migration history, and run alembic revision --autogenerate against that one. At deploy time, loop over tenants and call alembic upgrade head (applying the already-authored migration script) against each tenant's connection string - not autogenerate - so there's no per-tenant schema comparison at all. Your "Target database is not up to date" error happens because autogenerate refuses to diff a DB whose alembic_version isn't already stamped at the latest known revision; that check becomes irrelevant once you separate "author migrations against one reference DB" from "apply migrations to N tenant DBs". In env.py, parametrize the target connection (e.g. via -x tenant=<id> or an env var) so the same generated scripts run unmodified across all tenants.

question:
How to map element from one list to all elements in a sub-list to form a list of tuples (coordinates)

I am trying to map each element[x] from list: rows to all elements of the sub-list[x] from another list: cols and the result should be a list of tuples. These 2 lists, rows and cols have the same length, each element in rows will correspond to a sub-list(of various length) in list cols. The output should be a list of tuples in which each tuple will have the elements mapped/zipped : (row[0], cols[0][0]), (row[0], cols[0][1]), (row[1], cols[1][0]) and so on... Example input: rows = [502, 1064, 1500] cols = [[555, 905], [155, 475], [195, 595, 945]] Desired output: mapped = [(502, 555), (502, 905), (1064, 155), (1064, 475), (1500, 195), (1500, 595), (1500, 945)]
llm_attempt:
A single nested comprehension does this directly:

mapped = [(r, c) for r, sub in zip(rows, cols) for c in sub]

zip(rows, cols) pairs each row value with its corresponding sub-list; the inner for c in sub then unpacks that sub-list into individual tuples (r, c), one per element - exactly the (row[i], cols[i][j]) pattern you want, and it naturally handles cols sub-lists of different lengths without any extra bookkeeping.

question:
3D reconstruction from multiple depth maps

I'm working on reconstructing a 3D object from multiple depth maps taken at different angles. The object is rotating on a turntable, and the hyperspectral camera is stationary. The depth data is stored in a 570x570 2D array for each photo, and I'm using rotation matrices to align the points. I'm running into issues with overlap and incorrect rotations when trying to merge the depth maps. The code to extract the depth information for every pixel from the camera works, but I'm struggling with properly aligning and merging the depth maps. How can I fix the rotation and merging of depth maps to get a correct 3D model? Note: I'm working in Python. Should I use something else than rotation matrices? This is the point where I've got now. I'm able to convert the datacubes (that the hyperspectral camera generates after taking a picture), into 2D depth maps. The next step in my code will be to merge the depth maps into a 3D-shape, but that's where I'm stuck. Code: import numpy as np import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D # Settings num_pictures = 10 # This is a choice of the user. rotation_angle = 360 / num_pictures # Angle difference per picture image_size = 570 # 2D-array is 570x570 camera_distance = 162 # Depth distance from camera to rotation-axis / center of object # Simulate a object_distance_map (dummy data for tests) object_distance_map = np.random.uniform(100, 300, (image_size, image_size)) object_distance_map -= camera_distance # Correctie toepassen # Assenstelsel define x_range = np.linspace(-image_size // 2, image_size // 2, image_size) y_
reference_answer: You can estimate the surface using the alpha shape method in open3d . The example below is for a point cloud distribution that is similar to yours, but using fewer points and normalised coordinates. The raw 3D point cloud used for testing, coloured by camera angle: Surface reconstructed using the alpha shape method: Also visualised using trimesh (more responsive interactivity compared to matplotlib ): The main part of the code takes your entire point cloud all_points and uses it to instantiate an open3d PointCloud object, o3d_point_cloud : # ---- To open3d point cloud object ---- o3d_point_cloud = open3d.geometry.PointCloud() o3d_point_cloud.points = open3d.utility.Vector3dVector(all_points) The surface normals are estimated and aligned before reconstructing the surface. Tune alpha= to get a tighter fit (small alpha ) or a more regularised/smoother fit (larger alpha ). # Estimate normals prior to surface recon o3d_point_cloud.estimate_normals() o3d_point_cloud.orient_normals_consistent_tangent_plane(k=100) # Surface reconstruction using alpha shape mesh = open3d.geometry.TriangleMesh.create_from_point_cloud_alpha_shape( o3d_point_cloud, alpha=0.07 ) mesh.compute_vertex_normals() I finally smooth the resulting mesh: mesh = mesh.filter_smooth_simple(number_of_iterations=2) Reproducible example Imports and data for testing: import numpy as np #Static pyplots %matplotlib notebook #Interactive pyplots # %matplotlib widget import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d.art3d import Poly3DCollection import open3d # ---- Image settings ---- num_pictures = 7 #Angle differ
llm_attempt: With only a coarse camera_distance and no real intrinsics/calibration, plain rotation-matrix alignment will drift. Two likely culprits: (1) rotating about the array's geometric center instead of the true physical turntable axis - you need to translate points so the rotation axis sits at the origin, rotate by the known per-shot angle, then translate back; (2) treating pixel (x,y) grid positions as metric coordinates without passing them through the camera's actual intrinsics/projection model first, which distorts the point cloud before rotation is even applied. Rather than hand-rolling this, convert each depth map to a point cloud with correct intrinsics (e.g. Open3D's create_from_depth_image), apply your known turntable rotation as an initial guess, then refine with ICP (open3d.pipelines.registration.registration_icp) to correct residual calibration/axis error before merging. Open3D also provides voxel downsampling and outlier removal to clean up overlap once merged. Rotation matrices aren't wrong in principle, just insufficient alone without exact calibration - ICP-based registration is the standard fix for real, non-simulated data like this.

question:
Why does a function seem to be executed more times than the number of elements passed to np.vectorize(function)?

I am looking into numpy.vectorize . I define a function f , which takes an input, prints hi {input} , and returns the input unmodified. import numpy as np def f(x): print(f"hi {x}") return x When I call: print(np.vectorize(f)(["input"])) I expect to get: hi input ['input'] However, I get: hi input hi input ['input'] It seems that f is executed twice, despite the np.vectorize receiving a list of length 1. How do I explain the seemingly too many executions of the vectorized function? In other, words, more specific to this exact scenario: I'd like to know why I get hi input twice.
reference_answer: The function is called twice to determine the number of outputs. numpy.vectorize documentation ( Notes ): If neither otypes nor signature are specified, then a call to the function with the first argument will be used to determine the number of outputs. The results of this call will be cached if cache is True to prevent calling the function twice. However, to implement the cache, the original function must be wrapped which will slow down subsequent calls, so only do this if your function is expensive. Specifying the type will prevent the second call: print(np.vectorize(f, otypes=[object])(["input"])) Setting cache to True : print(np.vectorize(f, cache=True)(["input"])) Those both output hi input ['input'] You can also specify the signature: print(np.vectorize(f, signature="(m)->(m)")(["input"])) This will output hi ['input'] ['input'] Try it online!
llm_attempt:
This is documented np.vectorize behavior: without otypes specified, it runs your function once on the first element as a "trial call" purely to determine the output dtype (it needs to know what dtype to allocate for the result array), then runs the real vectorized loop over every element - including that same first element again. So a length-1 input produces 2 calls total (1 probe + 1 real), and length-n produces n+1, with only the first element called twice. Avoid the extra call by telling vectorize the output type(s) up front, which skips the dtype-probing step entirely:

np.vectorize(f, otypes=[object])(["input"])

(use whatever dtype matches your actual return type, e.g. otypes=[float] for numeric output). With otypes given, f is called exactly once per input element.

question:
Convert JSONC to JSON via regex

I have JSONC as input (it is a superset of JSON that supports comments like //this one and /* this one */ ), and want to transform it into normal JSON (standard) using Python regex, but I'm not sure this can be solved with regex only. I know it can be done via semantic processing, maybe something like tree-sitter, but I'm looking for a regex-based solution. Since we don't use /* */ it's fine to have a regex only with removing comments with //. Note that: It is guaranteed that when you properly remove everything that's in the comments, you get valid JSON; The input is always pretty-formatted; Here is an example input with a failing sed attempt at the top: //tried this sed -r 's#\s//[^}]*##' // also tried this '%^*3//s39()' [ { "test1" : "http://test.com", "test2" : "http://test.com",//test // any thing "ok" : 3, //here 2 "//networkpath1" : true, //whynot "//networkpath2" : true // ok },//eof { "statement" : "I like test cases" }//eof ] Here is another failing attempt: comment_re = re.compile(r'\s//[^}]*') cleaned = comment_re.sub('', jsonStr) This removes too much when // occurs in a string literal. How can I make this work also for such inputs? NB: A solution is already helpful if it doesn't deal with /* this type of comments */ so no need to cover for that.
reference_answer: You could match quoted strings as a capture group and re-inject those in the result, so to avoid that you would match any of the comment delimiters in such strings: comment_re = re.compile( r'//.*|/\*[\s\S]*?\*/|("(\\.|.)*?")', # capture group for quoted strings ) cleaned = comment_re.sub(r'\1', jsonStr) # re-inject quoted strings Here it is not a requirement that the JSONC input be formatted with specific indentation and line separators.

question:
How to measure plant length in pixels using PlantCV

I am trying to use PlantCV to track the growth of seedlings, I am currently trying to get it to work on a single seedling before scaling it to track the growth of multiple seedlings. After some image processing I was able to remove all the noise from my image and am now left with this image of the single seedling. Can someone please guide me on where I should go from here? Original Image Image after thresholding and focusing on a region of interest Another example of a region of interest that contains secondary roots I intentionally cut out the leaves from my region of interest as I am only interested in the growth of the roots of the seedling import os import cv2 import numpy as np import pandas as pd import plantcv.plantcv as pcv pcv.params.debug = "plot" IMAGE_DIR = "TestPhotos" # Folder containing sequential images of seedlings OUTPUT_DIR = "results" RESULTS_CSV = os.path.join(OUTPUT_DIR, "growth_data.csv") # Create output folder os.makedirs(OUTPUT_DIR, exist_ok=True) # Initialize a results list results = [] for img_name in sorted(os.listdir(IMAGE_DIR)): if not img_name.lower().endswith(('.jpg', '.png', '.jpeg', '.tif')): continue # Load image img_path = os.path.join(IMAGE_DIR, img_name) img, path, filename = pcv.readimage(img_path) # Convert to HSV and extract the green channel to isolate plants hsv = pcv.rgb2gray_hsv(img, 'v') # Otsu thresholding bin_mask = pcv.threshold.otsu(gray_img=hsv, object_type="light") # Clean up small noise cleaned_mask = pcv.fill(bin_img=bin_mask, size=40) # cleaned_mask = pcv.erode(gray_img=cleaned_mask, ksize=2, i=2) # Define ROI rect_roi
llm_attempt:
From a clean binary mask, the standard PlantCV route to a length measurement is the morphology submodule: skeletonize, prune spurious spurs, then measure path length along the skeleton (exact argument names shift a bit by PlantCV version, but the pipeline is stable):

skel = pcv.morphology.skeletonize(mask=cleaned_mask)
pruned, seg_img, edge_objects = pcv.morphology.prune(skel_img=skel, size=N, mask=cleaned_mask)
seg_img2, labeled = pcv.morphology.segment_skeleton(skel_img=pruned, mask=cleaned_mask)
pcv.morphology.segment_path_length(segmented_img=seg_img2, objects=labeled, label="root")

segment_path_length stores each segment's pixel length in pcv.outputs.observations; sum the segments for total root length if it's one unbranched root, or keep them separate for the branched image. Tune the prune size threshold visually (debug="plot") so it removes fill() leftovers without cutting real root tips. For real-world units instead of pixels, include a reference object of known size in-frame and convert via that pixel-to-cm ratio.

question:
How reload plugin automatically after installing in the startup.py script

In my startup.py script I run code to install a plugin based on a zip file and the plugin is extracted succesfully to the path location where QGIS looks at to find plugins. During the same QGIS session, the button for the plugin is not shown and based on qgis.utils.active_plugins it appears that the plugin is not yet active. When I close the current QGIS session and open a new QGIS session, the plugin is now active and shown as a button. However, it would be less confusing to the user to if the plugin is simply already shown, since I write log messages that the plugin is installed. So some users might start looking for the plugin, while the plugin is not yet available. Are there PyQgis functions that automatically update the active plugins and reload plugins? Below is my current startup.py script from qgis.utils import iface from PyQt5.QtCore import QTimer from qgis.PyQt.QtCore import QSettings, QStandardPaths from qgis.core import QgsMessageLog, Qgis import zipfile import os import shutil # Automatically detect the user's home directory USER_HOME = os.path.expanduser("~") # Folder containing the ZIP files LOCAL_ZIP_FOLDER = os.path.join( USER_HOME, "Programs", "QGIS 3.40.8", "plugins", "Standaard actief" ) # Plugins to install PLUGIN_LIST = [ 'tools'#, ] def plugin_dir(): base = QStandardPaths.standardLocations(QStandardPaths.AppDataLocation)[0] return os.path.join(base, "profiles", "default", "python", "plugins") def install_from_zip(plugin_name): zip_path = os.path.join(LOCAL_ZIP_FOLDER, plugin_name + ".zip") target_dir = os.path.join(plugin_dir(), plugin_name) if not os
reference_answer: I'd take a look at the plugin_reload plugin which reloads a plugin during development to save having to restart QGis every time. It looks like this function contains the magic: \# Try to initially load the selected plugin if not loaded yet if plugin not in qgis.utils.plugins: qgis.utils.loadPlugin(plugin) qgis.utils.startPlugin(plugin) qgis.utils.updateAvailablePlugins() Is probably the key bit,
llm_attempt:
Extracting the zip only puts files on disk; QGIS won't pick up a new plugin until it's actually loaded and started in the running session. After extraction, call:

import qgis.utils
qgis.utils.loadPlugin(plugin_name)
qgis.utils.startPlugin(plugin_name)

loadPlugin imports the plugin module and registers it in qgis.utils.plugins/active_plugins; startPlugin calls its initGui(), which is what actually creates the toolbar button/menu entry - this is the same pair of calls the Plugin Manager itself triggers when a user installs and enables a plugin without restarting. If you also want it enabled on future normal startups (not just this session), make sure the QSettings key "PythonPlugins/<plugin_name>" ends up set to true, which startPlugin/the plugin manager flow normally handles automatically. Make sure extraction has fully finished (files written, __init__.py present with a valid classFactory) before calling loadPlugin, or the import can silently fail on that first attempt.

question:
How to enforce per-passenger maximum ride time as a soft constraint in OR-Tools VRP?

I’m working on a Vehicle Routing Problem using Google OR-Tools. The context is that each “customer” (or passenger) has to be picked up and eventually delivered to a common destination (for example, a school in the morning, or from the school to home in the afternoon). What I need is a way to enforce or at least strongly encourage that: (Arrival time at destination) – (Pickup time of customer) ≤ MaxRideTime For example, each passenger should not spend more than 60 minutes on the vehicle. I already have: A Duration (time) dimension for travel times. Capacity constraints per vehicle. A route duration cap (e.g., max 3 hours per bus). What I’m struggling with is how to express the per-customer ride time constraint inside the OR-Tools RoutingModel: It depends on both the end cumul (at the route’s final stop) and the pickup cumul for each customer. OR-Tools’ Routing API lets me set soft/hard bounds on individual cumul vars, but not directly on a difference like (End – Pickup). I would like the solver to prefer solutions where all customers have ride times ≤ 60 minutes (soft constraint, penalize violations), but I’m not sure what the best modeling strategy is. Has anyone modeled this before? Is there a clean way to add a soft penalty for (end – pickup) directly in OR-Tools? Do I need to introduce auxiliary variables with big-M constraints? Or is there another approach (multi-stage solving, custom dimensions, etc.) that works better? Any ideas, patterns, or references would be really helpful. Thanks! data = self._create_data_model(route_id, is_am) if not data: print("Failed to creat
reference_answer: It was answered a long time ago, I believe on the or-tools-discuss@ mailing list. Something like a soft lower bound on the cumul var of the pickup with target the end of day, and a soft upper bound on the delivery part with target the start of day. This will add a large constant part to the cost, but the effect is what you want.
llm_attempt:
Rather than combining two CumulVars from your existing Duration dimension after the fact, give ride time its own dimension that resets to 0 at each pickup. Add a second dimension with the same per-arc transit (travel + service time) as Duration, then force its cumul to 0 exactly at every pickup node:

routing.solver().Add(ride_dim.CumulVar(pickup_index) == 0)

for each pickup in your pickup-delivery pairs. After that, ride_dim's cumulative value at each delivery node directly equals that passenger's ride time (pickup-to-delivery elapsed time) as a normal CumulVar - so you can use the built-in soft-bound support directly, no big-M or auxiliary max() needed:

ride_dim.SetCumulVarSoftUpperBound(delivery_index, 60, penalty_coefficient)

This "reset at node" trick is the same pattern used for things like distance-since-refueling in OR-Tools' own examples, adapted to pickup-delivery ride time. Tune penalty_coefficient to control how strongly violations are discouraged relative to your other objective terms.

question:
Using matplotlib to build report of survey responses, what is the most efficient way to tally likert scores?

I am building out functionality in an existing app for a user to upload an excel file to plot out responses for survey questions. There are 4 likert questions with 2 comment response question. The relevant data is organized as such: Q1 Q2 Q3 Q4 Q5 Q6 0 Occasionally Agree Agree comment comment Very Well 1 Frequently Agree Agree NaN NaN Moderately 2 Frequently Agree Agree NaN NaN Well 3 Frequently Agree Neither Agree nor Disagree comment comment Moderately Currently, I do the following to build a list of all the questions, their listed responses, the 'type' of likert scale it is, and the amount each response is recorded per question. def read_responses(xl): responses = [] action = False data = pd.read_excel(xl) for name, values in data.items(): if name.endswith("?"): action = True if action == True: data_set = {} set = values.value_counts(dropna=True).to_dict() labels, data = list(set.keys()), list(set.values()) data_set['question'] = name data_set['type'] = id_type(labels) data_set["responses"] = labels data_set["values"] = data responses.append(data_set) build_chart(responses) This loops through the dataframe, skips the first few columns of system generated information, and then starts to count the values of each individual value in each row and assigns its count to separate a separate list which later get sent off to matplotlib for plotting along with each columns header to use as the title. In the end, this gets passed to my plotting function: [{'question': 'Q1', 'type': 'likert', 'responses': [Agree], 'values':[4] }] The type is determined based on the following function
reference_answer: The action flag you have there is a bit bizarre. I would go with one of the following instead: for name, values in data.items(): if not name.endswith("?"): continue data_set = {} set = values.value_counts(dropna=True).to_dict() ... Or for name, values in data.items(): if name.endswith("?"): data_set = {} set = values.value_counts(dropna=True).to_dict() ... Also, using set as a variable name is not ideal since it shadows the built-in set data type. The way you overwrite the data variable is also not ideal.
llm_attempt:
One real bug first: inside the loop you reassign the name data to a plain list (data_set["values"] = data, after labels, data = list(set.keys()), list(set.values())), which shadows your outer DataFrame data - so on the next iteration for name, values in data.items() breaks, since data is now a list. Rename the inner variable (e.g. counts), and set (a builtin) too. For the actual tallying, value_counts() is already the right, vectorized tool - nothing more "efficient" is needed. What's missing is consistent ordering: value_counts() sorts by frequency, not Likert order, and silently drops response options with zero count. Define the scale explicitly and reindex instead:

order = ["Never","Occasionally","Frequently","Always"]
counts = pd.Categorical(values.dropna(), categories=order, ordered=True)
counts = pd.Series(counts).value_counts().reindex(order, fill_value=0)

That guarantees consistent bar order across charts and includes zero-count categories.
